L28: TR97-005 | 17th February 1997 00:00
L29: #### On the Construction of Pseudo-Random Permutations: Luby-Rackoff Revisited
L30: 
L31: 【15†Image: Contact】
L32: 
L33: 【16†Image: Add Comment】
L34: 
L35: 【17†TR97-005】 Authors: 【18†Moni Naor】, 【19†Omer Reingold】
L36: Publication: 19th February 1997 13:27
L37: Downloads: 4829
L38: 
L39: Keywords:
L40: 
L41: 【20†Block-Ciphers】, 【21†encryption】, 【22†Permutations】, 【23†Private-key】, 【24†Pseudo-Randomness】
L42: 
L43: Abstract:
L44: Luby and Rackoff showed a method for constructing a pseudo-random
L45: permutation from a pseudo-random function. The method is based on
L46: composing four (or three for weakened security) so called Feistel
L47: permutations each of which requires the evaluation of a pseudo-random
L48: function. We reduce somewhat the complexity of the construction
L49: and simplify its proof of security by showing
L50: that two Feistel permutations are sufficient together with initial
L51: and final pair-wise independent permutations.
L52: The revised construction and proof provide a framework in which
L53: similar constructions may be brought up and their security can
L54: be easily proved.
L55: We demonstrate this by presenting some additional adjustments
L56: of the construction that achieve the following:
L57: 1. Reduce the success probability of the adversary.
L58: 2. Provide a construction of pseudo-random permutations with large
L59: input size using pseudo-random functions with small input size.
L60: 3. Provide a construction of a pseudo-random permutation
L61: using a single pseudo-random function.
L62: * * *

L0@P0: A Parallelizable Enciphering Mode
L1@P0: Shai Halevi∗ Phillip Rogaway†
L2@P0: June 17, 2003
L3@P0: Abstract
L4@P0: We describe a block-cipher mode of operation, EME, that turns an n-bit block cipher into
L5@P0: a tweakable enciphering scheme that acts on strings of mn bits, where m ∈ [1..n]. The mode is
L6@P0: parallelizable, but as serial-efficient as the non-parallelizable mode CMC [6]. EME can be used
L7@P0: to solve the disk-sector encryption problem. The algorithm entails two layers of ECB encryption
L8@P0: and a “lightweight mixing” in between. We prove EME secure, in the reduction-based sense of
L9@P0: modern cryptography. We motivate some of the design choices in EME by showing that a few
L10@P0: simple modifications of this mode are insecure.
L11@P0: Key words: Block-cipher usage, cryptographic standards, disk encryption, modes of operation,
L12@P0: provable security, sector-level encryption, symmetric encryption.
L13@P0: ∗IBM T.J. Watson Research Center, P.O. Box 704, Yorktown Heights, NY 10598, USA, shaih@watson.ibm.com

L16@P0: of Computer Science, Faculty of Science, Chiang Mai University, 50200 Thailand, rogaway@cs.ucdavis.edu

L31@P2: Tweakable enciphering schemes and their use. A tweakable enciphering scheme is a function E that maps a plaintext P into a ciphertext C = ET
L32@P2: K(P) under the control of a key K and
L33@P2: tweak T. The ciphertext must have the same length as the plaintext and there must be an inverse DT
L34@P2: K to ETK. We are interested in schemes that are secure in the sense of a tweakable, strong
L35@P2: pseudorandom-permutation (±prp): an oracle that maps (  T,P) into ET
L36@P2: K(P) and maps (T,C) into
L37@P2: DT
L38@P2: K(C) must be indistinguishable (when the key K is random and secret) from an oracle that
L39@P2: realizes a T-indexed family of random permutations and their inverses. A tweakable enciphering
L40@P2: scheme that is secure in the ±prp-sense makes a desirable tool for solving the disk-sector encryption 
L41@P2: problem: one stores at disk-sector location T the ciphertext C = ET
L42@P2: K(P) for plaintext P. The IEEE
L43@P2: Security in Storage Working Group [8] plans to standardize a ±prp-secure enciphering scheme. 
L44@P2: Our contribution. This paper specifies EME, which is a simple and parallelizable tweakable
L45@P2: enciphering scheme. The scheme is built from a block cipher, such as AES. By making EME parallelizable we accommodate ultra-high-speed mass-storage devices to the maximal extent possible
L46@P2: given our security goals. When based on a block cipher E: {0, 1}k ×{0, 1}n →{0, 1}n our mode
L47@P2: uses a k-bit key and 2m+1 block-cipher calls to encipher an mn-bit plaintext in a way that depends
L48@P2: on an n-bit tweak. We require that m ∈ [1..n].
L49@P2: The name EME is meant to suggest ECB-Mix-ECB, as enciphering under EME involves ECBencrypting the plaintext, a lightweight mixing step, and another ECB-encryption. For a description
L50@P2: of EME look ahead to Figures 1 and 2.
L51@P2: We prove that EME is secure, assuming that the underling block cipher is secure. The proof
L52@P2: is in the standard, provable-security tradition: an attack on EME (as a ±prp with domain  M =
L53@P2: {0, 1}n ∪{0, 1}2n ∪···∪{0, 1}n2
L54@P2: ) is shown to imply an attack on the underlying block cipher (as a
L55@P2: strong PRP with domain {0, 1}n).
L56@P2: We go on to motivate some of the choices made in EME by showing that other choices would
L57@P2: result in insecure schemes. Finally, we suggest an extension to EME that operates on sectors that
L58@P2: are longer than mn bits.
L59@P2: Cmc mode. The EME algorithm is follow-on work to the CMC method of Halevi and Rogaway [6].
L60@P2: Both modes are tweakable enciphering schemes built from a block cipher E: {0, 1}k ×{0, 1}n →
L61@P2: {0, 1}n. But CMC is inherently sequential, as it is built around CBC encryption and decryption.
L62@P2: EME was designed to overcome this limitation, which was seen as potentially problematic for highspeed encryption devices. The change does not increase the serial complexity; both modes use
L63@P2: 2m + 1 block-cipher calls (and little additional overhead) to act on an mn-bit messages.
L64@P2: Further history. Naor and Reingold gave an elegant approach for making a strong PRP on N
L65@P2: bits from a block cipher on n<N bits [13, 14]. Their approach involves a hashing step, a layer
L66@P2: of ECB encryption (say), and another hashing step. They do not give a fully-specified mode, but
L67@P2: they do show how to carry out the hashing step given an xor-universal hash-function that maps N
L68@P2: bits to n bits [13]. In practice, instantiating this object is problematic: to compare well with CMC
L69@P2: or EME one should find a construction that is simple and has a collision bound of about 2−128 and
L70@P2: is more efficient, in both hardware and software, than AES. No such construction is known.
L71@P2: An early, unpublished version of the CMC paper contained buggy versions of the CMC and
L72@P2: EME algorithms. Joux discovered the problem [9] and thereby played a key role in our arriving
L73@P2: at a correct solution. CMC was easily fixed in response to Joux’s attack, but EME did not admit
L74@P2: a simple fix. (Indeed, Section 6.1 effectively proves that no “simple fix” is possible for the earlier
L75@P2: buggy EME construction).
L76@P2-3: 1Efforts to construct a block cipher with a large blocksize from one with a smaller blocksize go
L77@P3: back to Luby and Rackoff [12], who also put forward the notion of a PRP and a strong PRP. The
L78@P3: concrete-security treatment of PRPs that we use begins with Bellare, Kilian, and Rogaway [2]. The
L79@P3: notion of a tweakable block-cipher is due to Liskov, Rivest, and Wagner [11]. The first attempt
L80@P3: to directly construct an mn-bit block cipher from an n-bit one is due to Zheng, Matsumoto, and
L81@P3: Imai [15]. A different approach is to build a wide-blocksize block-cipher from scratch, as with
L82@P3: BEAR, LION, and Mercy [1, 4].
L83@P3: Discussion. EME has some advantages over CMC beyond its parallelizability. First, it uses a
L84@P3: single key for the underlying block cipher, instead of two keys. All block-cipher calls are keyed by
L85@P3: this one key. Second, enciphering under EME uses only the forward direction of the block cipher,
L86@P3: while deciphering now uses only the backwards direction. This is convenient when using a cipher
L87@P3: such as AES, where the two directions are substantially different, as a piece of hardware or code
L88@P3: might need only to encipher or only to decipher. Finally, we prove EME secure as a variable-inputlength (VIL) cipher and not just as a fixed-input-length (FIL) one. This means that, in an attack,
L89@P3: the adversary may intermix plaintexts and ciphertexts of various lengths.
L90@P3: We comment that the parallelizability goal is arguably of less utility for a ±prp-secure enci- 
L91@P3: phering scheme than for some other cryptographic goals. This is because, parallelizable or not,
L92@P3: a ±prp-secure encryption scheme cannot avoid having latency that grows with the length of the 
L93@P3: message being processed (to achieve the ±prp security notion one cannot output a single bit of 
L94@P3: ciphertext until the entire plaintext has been seen). Still, parallelizability is useful even here, and
L95@P3: the user community wants it [7]. More broadly, EME continues a tradition of trying to make
L96@P3: modes of operation (like CTR mode and PMAC [3]) that achieve parallelizability at near-zero
L97@P3: added computational cost compared to their intrinsically serial counterparts.

L163@P4: 3 Specification of EME
L164@P4: We construct from block cipher E: K×{0, 1}n →{0, 1}n a tweakable enciphering scheme that we
L165@P4: denote by EME[E] or EME-E. The enciphering scheme has key space K, the same as the underlying
L166@P4: cipher, and tweak space is T = {0, 1}n. The message space M = {0, 1}n ∪{0, 1}2n ∪···{0, 1}n2
L167@P4: contains any string having any number m of n-bit blocks, where m ∈ [1..n]. An illustration of
L168@P4: EME mode is given in Figure 2. In the figures, all capitalized variables except for K are n-bit strings
L169@P4: (key K is an element of the key-space K). Variable names P and C are meant to suggest plaintext
L170@P4: and ciphertext. When we write ET
L171@P4: K(P1 ··· Pm) we mean that the incoming plaintext P = P1 ··· Pm
L172@P4: is silently partitioned into n-bit strings P1,...,Pm and when we write DT
L173@P4: K(C1 ··· Cm) we mean
L174@P4: that the incoming ciphertext C = C1 ··· Cm is partitioned into n-bit strings C1,...,Cm. It is an
L175@P4: error to provide E with a plaintext that is not mn bits for some m ∈ [1 .. n], or to supply D with
L176@P4: a ciphertext that is not mn bits for some m ∈ [1..n].
L177@P4: 4 Security of EME
L178@P4: The following theorem relates the advantage an adversary can get in attacking EME[E] to the
L179@P4: advantage that an adversary can get in attacking the block cipher E.

L23: The Feistel-network is a popular structure underlying many block-ciphers where the cipher is constructed from many simpler rounds, each defined by some function which is derived from the secret key. Luby and Rackoff showed that the three-round Feistel-network – each round instantiated with a pseudorandom function secure against adaptive chosen plaintext attacks (CPA) – is a CPA secure pseudorandom permutation, thus giving some confidence in the soundness of using a Feistel-network to design block-ciphers.
L24: But the round functions used in actual block-ciphers are – for efficiency reasons – far from being pseudorandom. We investigate the security of the Feistel-network against CPA distinguishers when the only security guarantee we have for the round functions is that they are secure against non-adaptive chosen plaintext attacks (nCPA). We show that in the information-theoretic setting, four rounds with nCPA secure round functions are sufficient (and necessary) to get a CPA secure permutation.
L25: Unfortunately, this result does not translate into the more interesting pseudorandom setting. In fact, under the so-called Inverse Decisional Diffie-Hellman assumption the Feistel-network with four rounds, each instantiated with a nCPA secure pseudorandom function, is in general not a CPA secure pseudorandom permutation.
